item.title: World markets bounce back after a recovery for AI stocks on Wall Street
item.description: World shares and U.S. futures advanced Monday after artificial intelligence stocks recovered some ground lost in last week’s sell-offs.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: World shares and U.S. futures advanced Monday after artificial intelligence stocks recovered some ground lost in last week’s sell-offs. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX climbed 0.6 per cent to 25,974.42, and the CAC 40 in Paris was up 0.4 per cent, at 8,168.36. Britain’s FTSE 100 rose 0.4 per cent to 10,720.81. The future for the S&P 500 was up 0.3 per cent and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.6 per cent. Taiwan’s Taiex led gains in Asia with a 4.9 per cent jump, thanks to a rebound in computer chipmaker TSMC, which surged 4.7 per cent. Regional tech stocks benefited from Friday’s rally in the U.S., where AI stocks got some relief from their sell-offs earlier in the week on worries that Democratic victories in the midterm elections could slow construction of AI data centres, particularly in Texas. Voters across political parties say they are wary about AI and don’t like increases to power bills caused by data centres. Investors also are watching to see what the Democrats’ sweeping victories will mean for markets and the broader economy. Monday trading started out strong in Tokyo, where the Nikkei 225 index closed 2.3 per cent higher at 58,775.50. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron climbed 2.8 per cent, giving up bigger gains earlier in the day, while Advantest, which makes testing equipment, was up 1.3 per cent. SoftBank Group’s shares fell 4.2 per cent as the company maneuvered to salvage a US$5.4 billion robotics deal with Switzerland’s ABB that Chinese regulators have rejected. In South Korea, the Kospi fell back after rising in the morning, shedding 0.8 per cent to 5,018.85. Samsung Electronics Corp. gained 0.6 per cent and chipmaker SK Hynix rose 0.4 per cent. Those are very modest gains for companies whose share prices have yo-yoed as investors dumped and then snapped up AI-related shares over the past few weeks. Elsewhere in Asia, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged 0.1 per cent lower to 24,448.95. The Shanghai Composite index added 0.3 per cent to 3,660.79. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged 0.1 per cent higher to 9,029.70. On Friday, the S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and trimmed its loss for the week to 2.7 per cent, which was its worst since U.S. President Donald Trump shook markets in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.1 per cent. The relative steadiness halted what had been a worldwide tumble for stocks. Indexes dropped six per cent in Tokyo and in Seoul following Wall Street’s plunge on Thursday. Friday’s biggest lift for the S&P 500 came from Nvidia, the chip company that has become the face of the boom and possible bust of the AI frenzy. Its stock climbed 2.8 per cent, coming off drops of 9.3 per cent and 3.2 per cent. Nvidia said Sunday it was opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. That followed Huang’s acknowledgment that he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China. During a routine briefing Monday, China’s Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations, calling them a smear campaign against Beijing. Nvidia’s share price fell 4.1 per cent in premarket trading early Monday. Nvidia is a central player in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Its chips power many of the data centres and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China’s access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology. “The scrutiny surrounding Jensen Huang reaches far beyond a personal scandal, touching the increasingly sensitive intersection of U.S. technology leadership, China and national security,” Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management said in a commentary. Despite its recent gyrations, the S&P 500 is only 5.7 per cent below its all-time high, which was set last month. A report released Friday showed U.S. employers hired many more workers last month than economists expected, in the latest signal that the U.S. economy is chugging along despite high inflation. In other dealings early Monday, Brent crude oil, the international standard, slipped two per cent to $96.38 per barrel. U.S. benchmark crude fell 1.5 per cent to $89.56 per barrel. The U.S. dollar slipped to 158.09 Japanese yen from 158.36 yen late Friday. The euro rose to $1.1188 from $1.1142. Elaine Kurtenbach, The Associated Press

item.title: Thousands of goats could be slaughtered due to U.S. tariffs
item.description: Bruce and Sharon VandenBerg have been producing goat cheese since 1989, first on their farm in Lindsay, Ont., and now at a state-of-the-art facility that employs roughly 200 people.
item.dc:creator: Heather Wright
item.content:encoded: LINDSAY, Ont. – Bruce and Sharon VandenBerg have been producing goat cheese since 1989, first on their farm in Lindsay, Ont., and now at a state-of-the-art facility that employs roughly 200 people. Mariposa Dairy has grown exponentially over the years, but its future became uncertain in a matter of days. “It was announced on (Sept. 8) and the tariffs came in on September the 15th. We had six days notice, six days,” said Bruce VandenBerg. In September, U.S. President Donald Trump issued 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods, including goat dairy. Mariposa sends 80 per cent of its product south of the border, providing private-label products to companies like Costco and Trader Joe’s. The company says the tariffs are costing roughly $1 million a week, a cost being shouldered by everyone from the farms to the producers to the distributors. “Everybody’s trying to take a little piece of the pain in order to try to make this work,” said Mariposa Dairy CEO Mark Anderson. “So while Mariposa Dairy takes a big piece of the impact of the tariff, our distributors taking a piece, our suppliers are taking a piece. And that’s how we’re trying to make it work for the short term.” But the short term is now dragging into the long term, and while the company says it is not quite at a breaking point, it is getting close. “Most companies could just stop and cut their supply off,” said VandenBerg. “But we have 200 dairy goat farms that are relying on us to take their milk.” “The goats milk every day,” added Anderson. “So we got to keep taking the milk, and it needs to flow because it doesn’t have anywhere else to go.” Mariposa gets its milk from roughly 50,000 goats across the province. So far, the company has been able to keep its purchasing volumes the same, but if it has to reduce the amount of milk it purchases, farms would be forced to slaughter portions of their herds. “(If) this trade policy does not get figured out, there will be a lot of goats culled,” said farmer Gabe Benschop, who has about 800 goats. “There will be either firms going out of business or farmers having to cut back.” While Mariposa distributes its product across Canada, there is not enough demand here to absorb the amount of cheese it produces. Conversely, the United States does not produce enough goat milk to meet its domestic demand. “They probably need to import 30 to 35 per cent of their goat cheese in order to meet their demand,” said Anderson. One of Mariposa’s largest distributors is Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that is suing Trump and the U.S. government over the 50 per cent tariffs. Gellert typically imports about US$80 million of Canadian cheese into the United States each year. If that lawsuit is successful, the 50 per cent tariffs would be void. “I’m really hopeful that in the first part of the new year, common sense kicks into place,” said VandenBerg. “We expanded based on a 16-year CUSMA agreement, and here we are in year six,” he said, referring to the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement that was negotiated during Trump’s first term in office. But that lawsuit is not set to be heard until January and the company says it cannot sustain the status quo until then. “I mean, ideally, if they could negotiate a solution, it would be best,” said Anderson. “Failing that, we’re going to need some type of financial support, to make it through this.
